He thought it might be a cold and tried ibuprofen, but it only helped a little and temporarily. Now he's also feeling dizzy and nauseous, which goes away when he steps outside to shovel snow. That's interesting because being outside seems to relieve his symptoms, which might suggest something related to his environment. Looking at his medical history, he has hypertension, type II diabetes, and asthma. His medications include amlodipine (which is a calcium channel blocker for blood pressure), metformin and glimepiride (both for diabetes), and a fluticasone/salmeterol inhaler, which is for asthma. So, no recent changes in medications that I can tell. He's been living at his upstate cabin for five weeks and hasn't traveled elsewhere recently. He doesn't smoke or use illicit drugs, so those factors are out. His vitals are: temperature 99°F (which is a low-grade fever), blood pressure 130/78 (which is okay, maybe a bit low diastolic?), pulse 72, and O2 sat 98%. He's asymptomatic in the office, and the physical exam is unremarkable. So, no obvious signs of distress when he's sitting there. The labs show hemoglobin of 20 g/dL and hematocrit of 60%. That's elevated. Normal hemoglobin for men is around 13.5-17.5 g/dL, so 20 is definitely high. Hematocrit is also elevated, which makes sense because it's the packed cell volume. Leukocyte count is normal, and platelets are okay too. So, putting this together. The headaches and dizziness are concerning. The improvement when he's outside suggests it might be related to the environment. The elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit point towards polycythemia. Polycythemia can be primary (like in polycythemia vera, a myeloproliferative disorder) or secondary, meaning it's due to another cause. Secondary causes could include chronic hypoxia, dehydration, or erythropoietin-stimulating agents. He's living at a cabin in the upstate, which might be at a higher altitude, but I'm not sure how high.
